claim: The ventral hippocampus (vH) plays a crucial role in anxiety-related behaviour.
source: The ventral hippocampus (vH) plays a crucial role in anxiety-related behaviour and vH neurons increase their firing when animals explore anxiogenic environments.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript and citations to prior literature.

claim: vH neurons increase their firing when animals explore anxiogenic environments.
source: The ventral hippocampus (vH) plays a crucial role in anxiety-related behaviour and vH neurons increase their firing when animals explore anxiogenic environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing increased neuronal activity in anxiogenic locations.

claim: vH neurons exhibited remapping of activity, overrepresenting anxiogenic locations.
source: We recorded neuronal action potentials during task performance and found that vH neurons exhibited remapping of activity, overrepresenting anxiogenic locations.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Direction-dependent firing was homogenised by the anxiogenic experience.
source: Direction-dependent firing was homogenised by the anxiogenic experience.
evidence: This finding is supported by data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The activity of vH neurons predicted the extent of exploration of the anxiogenic location.
source: We further showed that the activity of vH neurons predicted the extent of exploration of the anxiogenic location.
evidence: This is supported by the SVM classifier analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: Anxiety-related firing does not solely depend on the exploration of anxiogenic environments, but also on intentions to explore them.
source: Our data suggest that anxiety-related firing does not solely depend on the exploration of anxiogenic environments, but also on intentions to explore them.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing that neuronal activity in closed arms predicts future exploration of open arms.

claim: At least 14% of people in the European Union suffer from anxiety disorders.
source: 12-month prevalence estimates on mental disorders show that at least 14% of people in the European Union suffer from anxiety disorders (Wittchen et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wittchen et al., 2011.

claim: Around 31% of people in the United States have experienced some type of anxiety disorders in their lifetime.
source: around 31% of people in the United States have experienced some type of anxiety disorders in their lifetime (Kessler et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kessler et al., 1994.

claim: Lesions in the vH induce anxiolysis during the exploration of elevated open arenas.
source: Lesions in the vH induce anxiolysis during the exploration of elevated open arenas (e.g. EPM) (Jimenez et al., 2018; Kjelstrup et al., 2002; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Neurons recorded in the vH showed increased firing in locations with elevated anxiety.
source: Neurons recorded in the vH showed increased firing in locations with elevated anxiety (Ciocchi et al., 2015; Jimenez et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Amygdala projections to the vH are specifically shaping anxiety-related behaviour during the exploration of an EPM.
source: amygdala projections to the vH are specifically shaping anxiety-related behaviour during the exploration of an EPM (Felix-Ortiz and Tye, 2014; Pi et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Felix-Ortiz and Tye, 2014 and Pi et al., 2020.

claim: The reciprocal connection from vH to BA is involved in the expression of context-dependent fear memories.
source: Similarly, the reciprocal connection (from vH to BA) is involved in the expression of context-dependent fear memories (Kim and Cho, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim and Cho, 2020.

claim: Information related to anxiety in the vH is directly routed to the mPFC.
source: Furthermore, information related to anxiety in the vH is directly routed to the mPFC (Ciocchi et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ciocchi et al., 2015.

claim: Synchronised activity in the vH-mPFC monosynaptically connected long-range circuit is essential for the expression of anxiety behaviour.
source: and synchronised activity in this monosynaptically connected long-range circuit (Adhikari et al., 2010; Adhikari et al., 2011) is essential for the expression of anxiety behaviour.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Adhikari et al., 2010 and 2011.

claim: Rats spent significantly more time in closed arms compared to open arms during EPM exploration.
source: The time spent in closed arms is significantly higher than in the open arms and the centre (p=9.5615e-10, p=9.5657e-10, respectively. One-way ANOVA, Tukey-Kramer for multiple comparisons, n=16 sessions).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A total of 98 individual neurons were isolated from vH recordings during EPM exploration.
source: While rats explored the EPM, we recorded neuronal activity in the vH with tetrodes (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and isolated individual spikes from different single neurons (n=98).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of neurons recorded.

claim: vH neurons exhibited preferential firing in the open arms, closed arms, or centre of the EPM.
source: We identified vH neurons with previously described activity patterns (Ciocchi et al., 2015), exhibiting preferential firing in the open arms, closed arms, or centre of the EPM (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and a citation to prior work.

claim: The peak firing activities of individual neurons spanned the entire maze even though the exploration of open arms was minimal.
source: We observed that the peak firing activities of individual neurons spanned the entire maze even though the exploration of open arms was minimal.
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The activity of vH neurons was concentrated around the centre of the maze when shuttling from one closed arm to the other one.
source: When plotting the peak firing density across the maze (normalised by the total number of neurons possibly firing in a spatial bin) the activity of vH neurons was concentrated around the centre of the maze when shuttling from one closed arm to the other one (Figure 1E, top, stars indicate bins with significant higher density; bootstrapping; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by density analysis shown in Figure 1E with statistical significance determined by bootstrapping.

claim: Open areas are relevant for the neuronal activity of the vH.
source: Even though the reduced number of entries to the open arms and exploration of open areas prevents a powerful statistic calculation, the observed effects imply that open areas are relevant for the neuronal activity of the vH.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed concentration of peak firing activity in open areas.

claim: The removal of sidewalls along the ELM induced anxiety behaviour.
source: Overall, the removal of sidewalls along the ELM-induced anxiety behaviour that evolved during single behavioural sessions according to the anxiety content of each maze configuration.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing differences in time spent in different arms during CO configuration.

claim: Rats spent significantly more time in the non-changing arm compared to the changing arm during CO configuration.
source: a significant difference was found in the configuration with sidewalls removed (CO exploration, p=1.45e-05, Wilcoxon signed-rank)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The time spent in the centre area was longer during CO exploration compared to CC or CT explorations.
source: The time spent in the centre area (11.5 cm around the middle of the track) was also longer during CO exploration compared to CC or CT explorations (Figure 2E, p=2e-05 and p=0.034 against CC and CT, respectively, one-way ANOVA, Turkey-Kramer for multiple comparisons)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A total of 133 neurons were recorded with tetrodes in the vH during ELM exploration.
source: We recorded a total of 133 neurons with tetrodes in the vH (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), while the rats were exposed to the different configurations of the ELM.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of neurons recorded.

claim: During CO exploration, the distribution of peak firing activity was skewed towards the open area.
source: During the CO exploration, the distribution of peak firing activity was skewed towards the open area.
evidence: This observation is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A higher proportion of peak firing activities was located on the open arm during CO configuration compared to CC configuration.
source: Then, when one half was opened, a remapping of the neuronal activity was induced towards the anxiogenic location. We observed a higher proportion of peak firing activities located on the open arm (Figure 3B left, p=0.0121, chi-square test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A larger proportion of neurons changed the location of their peak firing activity from a previously closed to a currently opened arm upon sidewall removal.
source: The difference in proportions between these two subpopulations was significant (Figure 3B, right, p=0.0066, chi-square test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No differences were found for the location and location changes of peak firing activity during the exploration of the CT configuration.
source: Importantly, no differences were found for the location and location changes of peak firing activity during the exploration of the CT configuration using a novel texture and visual cues in the closed arm (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Dynamic remapping of vH activity is contingent to the experience of anxiety rather than to a stimulus-enriched environment or novelty.
source: suggesting that dynamic remapping of vH activity is contingent to the experience of anxiety rather than to a stimulus-enriched environment or novelty.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between CO and CT configurations.

claim: The spiking activity of 49 neurons out of 133 (36.84%) was significantly modulated by the speed of the animal during the exploration of the CC configuration.
source: We found that the spiking activity of 49 neurons out of 133 (36.84%) was significantly modulated by the speed of the animal during the exploration of the CC configuration.
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis of the relationship between neuronal activity and running speed.

claim: 72 out of 133 neurons (54.14%) were significantly modulated by running speed during the exploration of the CO configuration.
source: Also, as expected, a higher number of neurons (72 out of 133, 54.14%) were significantly modulated by running speed during the exploration of the CO, in agreement with the speed changes related to the experience of an anxiogenic area.
evidence: This is based on GLM analysis and is consistent with behavioral changes in the anxiogenic condition.

claim: Even after correcting for speed influence, a significant proportion of vH neurons changed the location of their peak firing activities from the closed area to the open area after sidewall removal.
source: Repeating the same analysis as in Figure 3B and D we found that a significant proportion of vH neurons changed the location of their peak firing activities from the closed area to the open area after sidewall removal (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is supported by analysis using GLM residuals shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There is a prominent influence of the anxiogenic location in the neuronal activity irrespective of running speed.
source: These results suggest that even though there is a modulation by the speed of the animal, there is also a prominent influence of the anxiogenic location in the neuronal activity irrespective of running speed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of speed-corrected neuronal activity.

claim: 80 neurons (60.15%) were classified as putative pyramidal cells.
source: we divided the recorded neurons in putative pyramidal cells (n=80, 60.15%) and putative interneurons (n=24, 18.05%) by using a threshold for the though-to-peak latency and the firing rate (put. pyramidal cells >0.3 ms and <20 Hz, respectively; and put. interneurons ≤0.3 ms and ≥10 Hz, respectively. Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on spike shape and firing rate analysis.

claim: 24 neurons (18.05%) were classified as putative interneurons.
source: we divided the recorded neurons in putative pyramidal cells (n=80, 60.15%) and putative interneurons (n=24, 18.05%) by using a threshold for the though-to-peak latency and the firing rate (put. pyramidal cells >0.3 ms and <20 Hz, respectively; and put. interneurons ≤0.3 ms and ≥10 Hz, respectively. Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on spike shape and firing rate analysis.

claim: Similar tendencies in the open arm-associated activity were observed for both putative pyramidal cells and putative interneurons.
source: Similar tendencies in the open arm-associated activity were observed for both, putative pyramidal cells and putative interneurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: After removing all SWR-associated spikes, the same tendencies regarding open arm-associated activity were maintained.
source: To control for this effect, we removed all SWR-associated spikes from the analysis, which resulted still in the same tendencies regarding open arm-associated activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Both PiO and PiC neurons showed diminished spatial information when going from CC to CO configuration.
source: Interestingly, both PiO and PiC neurons showed similar properties: their spatial information diminished when going from a CC to a CO configuration (p=1.66e-05 for PiO and p=0.0074 for PiC, Wilcoxon signed-rank test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Both PiO and PiC neurons showed increased sparsity when going from CC to CO configuration.
source: while their sparsity and coherence increased (p=6.86e-05 and p=1.88e-05 respectively for PiO; p=9.68e-04 and p=2.86e-04 for PiC, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Both PiO and PiC neurons showed increased coherence when going from CC to CO configuration.
source: while their sparsity and coherence increased (p=6.86e-05 and p=1.88e-05 respectively for PiO; p=9.68e-04 and p=2.86e-04 for PiC, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: PiO spatial properties tended to be diminished compared to PiC neurons for both spatial information and sparsity.
source: However, PiO spatial properties tended to be diminished compared to PiC neurons for both spatial information (p=0.0130, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) and sparsity (p=0.0311, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Neurons that remapped from the closed arm in CC to the opened arm in CO showed significantly lower spatial information already in the CC configuration.
source: Concerning neurons that remapped from the closed arm in CC to the opened arm in the CO configuration, these neurons showed significantly lower spatial information and significantly higher sparsity (p=0.0029 and p=0.0016, respectively, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) already in the CC configuration, prior to the CO configuration, with respect to the other neurons that did not remap (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The CC2-CT remapping score was significantly higher than the CC-CO remapping score.
source: The CC2-CT remapping score was significantly higher than the CC-CO (p=0.0358, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: vH neurons exhibited direction-dependent difference in neuronal firing during CC configuration exploration.
source: When monitoring the activity of individual vH neurons recorded during the exploration of the CC configuration (Figure 5A), we expectedly observed a profound direction-dependent difference.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Direction-dependent neuronal firing of vH neurons became homogenised once the sidewalls were removed and rats explored the CO configuration.
source: However, this direction-dependent neuronal firing of the same vH neurons became homogenised, meaning that it was very similar in both directions, once the sidewalls were removed and the rats were exploring the CO configuration.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and statistical analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: The PFS index of animals exploring the CC configuration was significantly different from the PFS index of animals exploring the CO configuration.
source: As expected, the PFS index of animals exploring the CC configuration was significantly different from the PFS index of animals exploring the CO configuration (Figure 5B, left, p=7.53e-09, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The PFS indexes between the exploration of the CC2 configuration and the CT configuration were not significantly different.
source: The PFS indexes between the exploration of the CC configuration prior to the CT (called CC2) and the PFS indexes during the CT configuration were not significantly different (Figure 5B, right, median PFSCC2=–0.1279, median PFSCT = 0.0922).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: All the PFS values during the exploration of CC, CC2, and CT were significantly lower than during the exploration of the CO configuration.
source: In general, all the PFS values during the exploration of CC, CC2, and CT were significantly lower than during the exploration of the CO configuration, as seen in the cumulative distribution plots of the PFS (Figure 5C, CO vs CC, p=7.53e-09; vs CT, p=4.6e-05; and vs CC2, p=1.68e-07; Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The performance of the SVM was above chance levels (95th percentile) in 9 out of 12 sessions.
source: We found that during individual recording sessions, the performance of the SVM was above chance levels (95th percentile) in 9 out of 12 sessions.
evidence: This is supported by the SVM classification analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The animals' speed before entering the open arm was not different between proximal or distal run endpoints, except for one session.
source: However, we observed that the animals' speed before entering the open arm was not different between proximal or distal run endpoints, except for one session (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Correct prediction of several sessions using the SVM classifier was achieved for controls in which speed or SWR-associated activity was corrected.
source: In addition, correct prediction of several sessions using the SVM classifier was achieved for controls in which speed or SWR-associated activity was corrected and also when restricting the pairs to be either only putative pyramidal cell pairs, or putative interneuron pairs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The neuronal population activity was a good predictor of the extent of the exploration of the open location, even when rats explored the closed arm before entering to the open location.
source: The neuronal population activity was a good predictor of the extent of the exploration of the open location, even when rats explored the closed arm before entering to the open location.
evidence: This is supported by the SVM classification analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The neuronal activity in the closed arm, of neuronal pairs, was sufficient to infer whether rats would perform proximal or distal explorations of the open arm.
source: Indeed, the neuronal activity in the closed arm, of neuronal pairs, was sufficient to infer whether rats would perform proximal or distal explorations of the open arm (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the SVM classification analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Not only a direct experience of anxiety enhances neuronal activity in the vH, but also its anticipation without a direct confrontation to an anxiety-inducing situation.
source: Anxiety-related modulation of vH neuronal activity in both the closed and the open locations implies that not only a direct experience of anxiety enhances neuronal activity in the vH, but also its anticipation without a direct confrontation to an anxiety-inducing situation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that neuronal activity in closed arms predicts future exploration.

claim: Nine long Evans rats from Charles River Laboratories (male, 250–600 g) were used in the experiments.
source: In total, nine long Evans rats from Charles River Laboratories (male, 250–600  g), were kept in 12 hr light cycles during behavioural experiments (performed during the light cycle).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental subjects used.

claim: All experimental procedures were performed under an approved licence (66.009/0281-WF/V/3b/2015) of the Austrian Ministry of Science and the Medical University of Vienna.
source: All experimental procedures were performed under an approved licence (66.009/0281-WF/V/3b/2015) of the Austrian Ministry of Science and the Medical University of Vienna.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: An array of 12 independently movable, gold-plated (100–500 kΩ) wire tetrodes were implanted in the vH.
source: After removal of the dura mater, an array of 12 independently movable, gold-plated (100–500  kΩ) wire tetrodes (13 µm insulated tungsten wires, California Fine Wire, Grover Beach, CA) mounted in a custom-made microdrive (Miba Machine Shop, IST Austria) were implanted (dorso-ventral: –6.5 mm).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the recording methodology.

claim: The EPM consisted of two closed and two open arms with dimensions of 9×50 cm.
source: The EPM consisted of two closed (with protective sidewalls) and two open (without sidewalls) arms. The dimensions of the arms were 9×50 cm, the walls in the closed arms were 40 cm high, and the EPM was elevated 70 cm above the floor.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental apparatus.

claim: The ELM consisted of a linear track of 120 cm length and 8 cm in width, elevated by 105 cm above the ground.
source: The ELM consisted of a linear track of 120 cm length and 8 cm in width. The maze was elevated by 105 cm above the ground.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental apparatus.

claim: A reward of two 20 mg sugar pellets was given at both endpoints of the ELM.
source: A reward was given at both endpoints (two 20 mg sugar pellets).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental procedure.

claim: In total, 14 sessions were recorded from six rats in the ELM.
source: In total, 14 sessions were recorded from six rats in the ELM (SC65, SC67, SC68, SC70, HM15, HM16).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: 100% of the neurons showed higher correlation than 0.98 between the averaged spike shapes of the first third and last third of the recording.
source: Note that 100% of the neurons showed higher correlation than 0.98, implying that the spike shape is not changing between the start and the end of a recording.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: More than 90% of the neurons show an amplitude change between –0.5% and 0.5% from the amplitude at the start.
source: Note that more than 90% of the neurons show an amplitude change between –0.5% and 0.5% from the amplitude at the start.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Hippocampal place cells have been reported to exhibit direction-specific spatial modulation of activity as animals run along a linear maze.
source: Hippocampal place cells have been reported to exhibit direction-specific spatial modulation of activity as animals run along a linear maze (McNaughton et al., 1983; Muller et al., 1994; Royer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The dorsal hippocampus (dH) region is critical for the encoding of spatial information.
source: Motivated by the critical role of the dorsal hippocampus (dH) region in the encoding of spatial information (O'Keefe, 1976; O'Keefe and Nadel, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Keefe, 1976 and O'Keefe and Nadel, 2011.

claim: Global remapping is a phenomenon observed in the dH when animals move from one environment to a different one.
source: Global remapping is a phenomenon observed in the dH when animals move from one environment to a different one (Leutgeb et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leutgeb et al., 2005.

claim: Remapping of neuronal activity in a new environment is expected to be random and independent of a previously explored environment.
source: Nevertheless, remapping of neuronal activity in a new environment is expected to be random and independent of a previously explored environment (Gauthier and Tank, 2018; Leutgeb et al., 2005; Schlesiger et al., 2018), even when emotional contexts are introduced (Moita et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Novel environments elicit the activation of vH neurons to a similar extent as an aversive stimulus.
source: Previous work has shown that novel environments elicit the activation of vH neurons to a similar extent as an aversive stimulus (Graham et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Graham et al., 2021.

claim: Hippocampal place cells fire preferentially at reward locations during goal-directed tasks.
source: It has been previously demonstrated that hippocampal place cells fire preferentially at reward locations during goal-directed tasks (Dupret et al., 2010; Hok et al., 2007; Hollup et al., 2001; Jin and Lee, 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Global remapping is observed in the intermediate hippocampus due to motivational changes.
source: and global remapping is observed in the intermediate hippocampus due to motivational changes (Jin and Lee, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jin and Lee, 2021.

claim: Dorsal hippocampal place cells remap or partially remap in the presence of an aversive stimulus.
source: Dorsal hippocampal place cells were shown to remap or partially remap in the presence of an aversive stimulus (Kong et al., 2021; Moita et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Dorsal hippocampal place cells remap towards areas of aversive stimuli or threats.
source: or remap towards areas of aversive stimuli or threats (Schuette et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A subset of basal and BA neurons synchronize with or reactivate dorsal hippocampal neurons during aversive experiences.
source: by synchrony with or reactivation of a subset of basal and BA neurons (Girardeau et al., 2017; Kong et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Girardeau et al., 2017 and Kong et al., 2021.

claim: Non-aversive stimuli presented in the same context as aversive ones did not induce remapping in dorsal hippocampal neurons.
source: Interestingly, the non-aversive stimulus, presented in the same context as the aversive ones, did not induce remapping in dorsal hippocampal neurons (Moita et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2015), a similar effect to our observations in vH neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Moita et al., 2004 and Wang et al., 2015.

claim: The vH is strongly associated with anxiety, and the anxiogenic location represents a highly salient environment for vH-dependent computations.
source: Furthermore, the vH is strongly associated with anxiety, and the anxiogenic location represents a highly salient environment for vH-dependent computations (Bannerman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bannerman et al., 2014.

claim: Novelty induces rate remapping in hippocampal neurons.
source: Rate remapping was significantly more robust in the novel context than in the anxiogenic one, in line with the literature suggesting that novelty induces rate remapping in hippocampal neurons (Kaefer et al., 2019; Leutgeb et al., 2005; Rennó-Costa et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The neuronal dynamics within the vH are subjected to the experience of anxiety.
source: Overall, we provided evidence that the neuronal dynamics within the vH are subjected to the experience of anxiety.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: When an anxiogenic situation was encountered, vH neurons over-represented this location.
source: When an anxiogenic situation was encountered, vH neurons, first, over-represented this location (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Spatial properties of neurons with their main activity in the anxiogenic area were reduced.
source: Second, spatial properties of the neurons, with their main activity in the anxiogenic area, were reduced (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: vH neuronal activity was tuned to the anxiogenic environment, impairing previous direction-dependent neuronal activity manifesting in the absence of anxiety.
source: Third, vH neuronal activity was tuned to the anxiogenic environment, impairing previous direction-dependent neuronal activity manifesting in the absence of anxiety (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The neuronal activity of vH neurons reflected and predicted the exploration of an anxiogenic location.
source: Fourth, the neuronal activity of vH neurons reflected and predicted the exploration of an anxiogenic location (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: These results expand our view of vH function by highlighting dynamic and predictive computations during anxiety.
source: Collectively, these results expand our view of vH function by highlighting dynamic and predictive computations during anxiety.
evidence: This is a summary statement interpreting the significance of the findings.
